food.text: The Khazars dominated the Volga-Don steppes and Crimea from about 650 to 965. Unlike most nomadic peoples of the steppe, they built a self-sufficient economy that combined raising sheep and cattle for export, extensive farming, and heavy use of the Volga River's rich fishing stocks.

Long before Kievan Rus' emerged as a state, the Slavic tribes of the region were primarily agriculturalists, growing cereal grains and crops and raising livestock. They also traded with neighbors such as Volga Bolghar, Khazar Itil, and Byzantine Chersonesus. The most valuable commodities they traded were captive slaves and fur pelts, usually in exchange for silver coins or oriental finery.

In the 9th century, Rus' merchants traveling the Volga trade route toward the Middle East sold furs, honey, and slaves in exchange for Arabic silver dirhams. Some of this silver later turned up in hoards as far away as Sweden.
In the Old Russian period, bread, grains, and other starchy foods formed the main part of the diet. A loaf of bread and salt was always present during gatherings.

Women in the Old Russian period baked pies filled with ingredients such as mushrooms or berries. Kasha, made from grains like buckwheat and oats, was also common and was seen as a symbol of a household's wellbeing.

Even after Kievan Rus' adopted Christianity, many Slavic communities continued rituals honoring the deities Rod and the Rozhanitsy with offerings of bread, porridge, cheese, and mead. Christian clergy repeatedly condemned these offerings, but the practice persisted for generations.
Many people in the Old Russian period turned honey and berries into an early form of gingerbread. This sweet treat has remained so popular that it is still enjoyed as a dessert in Russia today.

The Khazars not only taxed goods passing through their territory but also produced isinglass, a substance made from fish, as one of their own exports. Their access to the Volga River's abundant fish stocks helped make this possible, alongside their farming and herding economy.

art.text: In 988 AD, Vladimir the Great led Kievan Rus' to convert to Orthodox Christianity from its earlier pagan religions. The monumental architecture that followed was mainly ecclesiastical, meaning it was built for the church.

According to legend, Kievan Rus' chose Orthodox Christianity over other religions because of the beauty of the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. If true, a single building's splendor shaped the religious and artistic direction of a whole realm.

The use and making of icons entered Kievan Rus' after its conversion to Orthodox Christianity from the Byzantine Empire in 988 AD. These icons strictly followed models and formulas hallowed by usage, some of which had originated in Constantinople.

Russian vernacular architecture stems from wooden construction traditions. Monumental masonry construction began to appear during the Kievan period, with much of the standing architecture from this era tied to Vladimir's conversion to Orthodox Christianity.

The style that dominated after 988 blended Slavic and Byzantine styles, with churches built in brick and stone. They were first built by imported Greek and Byzantine masters, but local craftsmen adopted the methods and slightly modified them.

Twentieth-century excavations of the Church of the Tithe showed that its original foundations follow a Byzantine inscribed cross plan. This plan, borrowed from Byzantine architecture, became the main prototype for Kievan masonry churches.

As the Byzantine prototype was adapted, Kievan masonry churches developed their own look. Compared with the Byzantine churches they were based on, they had more pronounced silhouettes, were bulkier, and had smaller windows, which gave them a more mysterious interior.

war.text: On June 18, 860, a fleet of about 200 Rus' vessels sailed into the Bosporus at sunset while Michael III and his navy were away, and began pillaging the suburbs of Constantinople. The attackers set homes on fire, drowning and stabbing the residents. They then raided the Isles of the Princes, plundering dwellings and monasteries and slaughtering those they captured, including twenty-two servants of the exiled former patriarch Ignatius of Constantinople, whom they took aboard a ship and dismembered with axes.

Under Krum the Bulgars inflicted a series of crushing defeats on the Byzantines in the early 9th century. In 809 Krum forced the surrender of Serdica and slaughtered its Byzantine garrison despite his promise of safe conduct. In 811 the Byzantine emperor Nikephoros I burned Pliska and ordered his army to kill its population, then was killed in the Vărbica pass along with many of his troops, and tradition says Krum had the emperor's skull lined with silver and used it as a drinking cup. After Krum died in 814, his son Omurtag negotiated a thirty-year peace treaty with the Byzantine Empire.

According to the Primary Chronicle, Oleg the Wise led a Rus' fleet against Byzantium in 907, landing a large army in Thrace to plunder it. The Byzantines then offered peace, and Oleg's campaign is confirmed by the surviving text of the resulting peace treaty.

Sviatoslav I, Prince of Kiev from 945 until his death in 972, was known for persistent campaigns in the east and south that precipitated the collapse of Khazaria and the First Bulgarian Empire. He conquered numerous East Slavic tribes, defeated the Alans and attacked the Volga Bulgars, at times allied with the Pechenegs and Magyars. His death came in an ambush by the Pechenegs near the Dnieper rapids early in 972, and according to the Primary Chronicle the Pecheneg khan made his skull into a chalice.

The Varangian Guard was an elite unit of the Byzantine army composed mainly of Norsemen and Rus' warriors who served as personal bodyguards to the emperors. Rus' fighters had served Byzantium as early as 874, and the Guard was formally established under Emperor Basil II in 988 after Vladimir I of Kiev sent him 6,000 men.

The 860 Rus' attack on Constantinople was provoked by the Byzantine construction of the fortress Sarkel, which restricted Rus' trade along the Don River in favor of the Khazars. Patriarch Photius described the assault as striking like a thunderbolt from heaven.

During the siege of Dorostolon, which lasted 65 days, John Kourkouas, a relative of the emperor, was killed, and the Rus' displayed his severed head from one of their towers. The Rus' and their Bulgarian allies were reduced to extremities by famine. To appease their gods, they drowned children in the Danube, but the sacrifices failed to improve their position.

Sviatoslav began by rallying the East Slavic vassal tribes of the Khazars to his cause. Those who would not join him, such as the Vyatichs, were attacked and forced to pay tribute to Kiev rather than to the Khazars. Proceeding by the Oka and Volga rivers, he attacked Volga Bulgaria with Oghuz and Pecheneg mercenaries, perhaps to counter the superior cavalry of the Khazars and Bulgars. He then destroyed the Khazar city of Sarkel around 965 and the Khazar capital of Atil, and a visitor to Atil wrote soon after: "The Rus' attacked, and no grape or raisin remained, not a leaf on a branch."

In summer 969, Sviatoslav invaded Bulgaria again with an army that included Pecheneg and Magyar troops, devastating Thrace, capturing the city of Philippopolis, and massacring its inhabitants. In summer 970 he crossed the Danube and laid siege to Adrianople, causing panic in the streets of Constantinople. The Byzantines sent commander Bardas Skleros, who defeated the coalition of Rus', Pechenegs, Magyars, and Bulgarians at the Battle of Arcadiopolis. Later, at Dorostolon, the Byzantines besieged Sviatoslav for sixty-five days, and according to the Primary Chronicle his camp on Berezan Island was then devastated by famine, so that even a horse's head could not be bought for less than a half-grivna.

The Varangians were Viking warriors, traders, and settlers from Sweden who, according to the Primary Chronicle, settled in Novgorod in 862 under Rurik. Rurik's relative Oleg conquered Kiev in 882, establishing the state of Kievan Rus'.

In 791, Byzantine emperor Constantine VI launched an expedition against Bulgaria to retaliate for incursions in the Struma valley since 789. Kardam met the Byzantine army near Adrianople in Thrace, defeating it and forcing it to flee.

Rus' warriors also served the Byzantines as mercenaries during this era. A squadron of 700 Rus' fought in the Byzantine Crete expedition of 902, and in 949 Rus' troops sailed on nine vessels to join another Greek expedition against the Emirate of Crete.

During the siege of Dorostolon the Rus' forces were reduced to near starvation, and some 2,000 warriors, including women, made a surprise sally out during the night to search for supplies. They defeated a Byzantine force on the way and later returned to the city. After the eventual defeat of the Rus', the Byzantines were astonished to find the bodies of armed women among the fallen warriors.

literature.text: The roots of Russian written literature reach back to the Early Middle Ages, when Old Church Slavonic was introduced as a liturgical language and came to be used as a literary language. The native Russian vernacular stayed in use for oral literature and for written decrees, laws, messages, chronicles and military tales.

Long before books, the East Slavic tribes kept a rich oral literature. It included pagan myths and prayers, zagovory (evocations), charms, byliny (heroic epics), legends, fairy tales and folksongs. By definition it is older than written literature, and it accompanied the written word throughout its development.

Old Russian "bookish" literature traces its beginnings to the introduction of Old Church Slavonic in Kievan Rus' as a liturgical language. This happened in the late 10th century, following Christianization. The East Slavs soon developed a literature of their own.

In Kievan Rus', chronicles and epic poetry were written in Old Church Slavonic, and oral folktales appeared alongside them. The common spoken language was Old East Slavic, which eventually divided into Ukrainian, Russian and Belarusian.

Scholars in the Preslav and Ohrid Literary Schools of Bulgaria created the Cyrillic script for their needs. Bulgarian scholars and works then spread Old Bulgarian, the Cyrillic alphabet and the Glagolithic alphabet to Kievan Rus' and other parts of the Slavic world.

Ukrainian literature has a thousand-year history that begins with the formation of Kievan Rus. Even in prehistoric times, before the ninth century, the ancestors of Ukrainians had a developed oral art.

The oldest dated manuscript of Early Russian, and of all Slavic literature, to survive is the Novgorod Codex, also called the Novgorod Psalter, written c. 1000. It was unearthed in 2000 at Veliky Novgorod and consists of four wooden tablet pages filled with wax.

politics.text: The traditional start date of specifically Russian history is 862, when the Rus' state was established in the north. Its rulers were Varangians. The story of Russia therefore begins with a ruling group of Scandinavian origin governing East Slavic lands.
In 882, Prince Oleg of Novgorod seized Kiev. This united the northern and southern lands of the Eastern Slavs under one authority. The two parts still kept significant autonomy from each other.

In 988 the Rus' state adopted Christianity from the Byzantine Empire. This began a synthesis of Byzantine, Slavic and Scandinavian cultures. That blend defined Russian culture for the next millennium.

Kievan Rus' became the largest and most powerful realm in Europe in the 10th and 11th centuries. It included much of present-day Ukraine, Belarus and the western part of European Russia. Only later did it break apart into rival regional powers.

Kievan Rus' was a coordinated group of princely states with a shared interest in keeping river trade going. It controlled the trade route for furs, wax and slaves between Scandinavia and the Byzantine Empire. That route ran along the Volkhov and Dnieper Rivers.

According to the Primary Chronicle, in 882 the pagan Prince Oleg conquered Kyiv from Askold and Dir. He proclaimed it the new capital of the Rus'. The city thus changed hands through conquest, not inheritance.

From the 10th century, the Russian lands were dominated by a noble class known as the boyars. Above them stood the grand prince, and much later the tsar. This noble class remained a fixture of Russian politics for centuries.
Byzantine sources called the early medieval Khazar state "eastern Tourkia", using the Greek name Tourkia. The same sources used "western Tourkia" for the medieval Hungarian state.

Kievan Rus' was made up of several principalities ruled by interrelated Rurikid princes, called kniazes. These relatives often fought one another for possession of Kyiv. Family ties did not guarantee peace.

The origins of Kievan Rus' remain obscure and uncertain. The Primary Chronicle says the Rus' people initially consisted of Varangians from Scandinavia. Anti-Normanist historians argue that East Slavic tribes along the southern Dnieper were already forming a state on their own.
The Varangian elite, including the ruling Rurik dynasty, later assimilated into the Slavic population. The Scandinavian-origin rulers of the Rus' gradually became part of the society they governed.

philosophy.text: In the Early Middle Ages, the lands of present-day Ukraine were home to different tribes who practised their traditional pagan religions. Byzantine Rite Christianity only became prominent around the turn of the first millennium.

In the 7th century, the steppe religion Tengrism was practised in part of present-day Ukraine. It belonged to Old Great Bulgaria, one of the different belief systems that existed here before Christianity became prominent.

The East Slavs became a prominent group in Europe between the 3rd and 8th centuries AD. This led to the establishment of Kievan Rus' in the 9th century. In 988 Kievan Rus' adopted Orthodox Christianity from the Byzantine Empire.

Saint Olga is described as the first recorded convert to Eastern Orthodoxy in the emerging state of Kievan Rus'. She visited Constantinople in either 945 or 957, as the state came increasingly under Byzantine cultural influence in the 10th century.
According to tradition, in the 980s Olga's grandson Vladimir had his people baptised in the Dnieper River. The story marks the moment when Kievan Rus' turned toward Eastern Orthodoxy.

culture.text: In the sixth and seventh centuries, the East Slavs of the Korchak culture lived in open settlements of ten to twenty rectangular, semi-subterranean dwellings. Each home had a stone furnace in one corner and held up to five people. A settlement had fewer than 100 people in all.

In the 10th century the emerging state of Kievan Rus' came increasingly under the cultural influence of the Byzantine Empire. Saint Olga, the first recorded convert to Eastern Orthodoxy, visited Constantinople in 945 or 957. According to tradition, her grandson Vladimir had his people baptised in the Dnieper River in the 980s.

The East Slavs gradually settled western Russia in two waves. One moved from Kiev toward present-day Suzdal and Murom, and another from Polotsk toward Novgorod and Rostov. The territory had earlier been populated by Finno-Ugrian peoples, and from the 7th century the incoming East Slavs slowly assimilated them.
The Korchak people buried their dead by cremation. They used kurgan burial mounds as well as flat-grave cemeteries, where the cremated remains were placed in urns.

The Luka-Raikovetska culture had large settlements in the Carpathian zone, such as Plisnesk, Roukhotine and Revne. It also had tribal-political centers, including Kyiv, which served as administrative, economic and religious centers of the population. From the 8th century the number of strongholds increased.

Written examples of Old East Slavic, also called Old Russian, are attested from the 10th century onwards. It belongs to the East Slavic languages, of which Russian, Belarusian and Ukrainian are living members.
The Korchak culture is characterized by modeled vessels with specific shapes and no decoration. They represent the first stage in the development of Slavic pottery.

Luka-Raikovetska pottery changed over time. Early vessels were stucco-made in the late 7th and 8th centuries, and partially wheel-made pottery appeared from 761, though usually in the 9th century. In the 10th century wheel-made pottery predominated, with conic pots, bowls and frying pans decorated with ornamental lines and bands.

Luka-Raikovetska cemeteries had cremation burials in pits and often in barrows. In the 8th to 10th centuries the wooden constructions in these barrows can be traced from the Dnieper to the Elbe. In the late stages, probably due to Christian influences, burial of unburnt bodies emerged.

In the Early Middle Ages the territories of present-day Ukraine supported different tribes practising their traditional pagan religions. One example was the Tengrism of Old Great Bulgaria in present-day Ukraine in the 7th century.
Judaism has existed in the territories of present-day Ukraine for approximately 2,000 years. After the 7th century it influenced the neighbouring Khazar Khaganate.
